title.en: Explain Katz's technical, human and conceptual skills

say.en: A shift supervisor in a factory, a regional sales head and the managing director all get work done through others. Yet their days look completely different. In this lesson: Explain who a manager is.
Describe the levels of management.
Explain Katz's technical, human and conceptual skills.

body.en: A manager is a person who plans, organises, directs and controls the work of others to achieve the goals of the organisation. Top-level *managers* (board, chief executive, managing director) set objectives and overall policies and are responsible to owners and society. Middle-level managers (heads of departments, regional managers) turn these policies into plans, coordinate departments and guide supervisors. First-line managers (supervisors, foremen) direct the workers directly and maintain quality and discipline.

say.en: A manager is a person who plans, organises, directs and controls the work of others to achieve the goals of the organisation. Top-level managers (board, chief executive, managing director) set objectives and overall policies and are responsible to owners and society. First-line managers (supervisors, foremen) direct the workers directly and maintain quality and discipline. Top: objectives, policies, long-term plans.
Middle: interpret policies, coordinate departments.
First-line: supervise workers, day-to-day operations.

say.en: On the board: Levels and skills.

body.en: Robert Katz identified three *skills*. Technical skill is knowledge of methods, tools and procedures of a specialised field, most needed at the first-line level. Human skill is the ability to work with, motivate and lead people, needed equally at all levels. Conceptual skill is the ability to see the organisation as a whole, understand how its parts relate, and think about the future; it matters most at the top. As a manager rises, the need for technical skill falls and the need for conceptual skill rises.

problem.en: Rekha is promoted from production supervisor to plant manager and later to director of operations. How does the mix of skills she needs change?

steps.en: As supervisor she relies most on technical skill: machines, processes, quality.
As plant manager she needs more human skill to coordinate several supervisors and departments.
As director she needs mostly conceptual skill: strategy, how operations fit the whole company.

answer.en: Technical skill falls and conceptual skill rises with each promotion; human skill remains important.
